newsitem.title: FRANCE: Many Corsican bombs due to gangs, not guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Many Corsican bombs due to gangs, not guerrillas.

text.p: Gangsters rather than separatist guerrillas have been behind many of almost 1,200 bomb attacks on the French Mediterranean island of Corsica in the past two years, a public prosecutor says.

"It's intolerable," prosecutor Jean-Pierre Couturier told the appeal court of Bastia in northern Corsica late on Monday, saying the island's 250,000 people were slipping into accepting violence as a part of life.

He said guerrillas fighting a 20-year-old campaign for more autonomy from mainland France claimed responsibility for just 148 of 574 bomb attacks in 1996. In 1995, the various guerrilla groups claimed responsibility for 154 of 602 bombings.
"Seventy-five per cent of the attacks can't be blamed on terrorist organisations but come from private or commercial disputes," Couturier said.

Nevertheless, police suspect rival nationalist groups are still responsible for many of the unclaimed attacks, often fighting over the spoils of local rackets. Such attacks are not registered in official statistics as political violence.
Bombers target government buildings ranging from post offices to police stations, private businesses and holiday complexes, mostly at night to avoid casualties.
The lack of casualties has meant the guerrillas have been taken less seriously than, for instance, the Irish Republican Army or the Basque ETA organisation.

On Tuesday, the Interior Ministry said that 15 members or sypathisers of the separatist group A Cuncolta Naziunalista were in custody after a string of raids in Corsica and in southern France on Monday.

"Arms and munitions were seized," it said in a statement after the crackdown, spurred by an inquiry into the bombing of a hotel complex in northern Corsica in October. Cuncolta is the legal wing of the outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front.
Magistrates say they hope an age-old tradition of silence in Corsica which prevents people from testifying against the guerrillas may at last be eroding.

Francois Santoni, head of Cuncolta, and his lawyer girlfriend Marie-Helene Mattei were placed under investigation last month for attempted extortion, complicity in bomb attacks and membership of a terrorist organisation.
Police said there were two new blasts during the night. They damaged an empty house and a driving school but caused no casualties.
The murder rate in Corsica is several times higher than in mainland France. In 1996, there were 22 killings on the island, down from 40 in 1995.
Fifteen political activists have been among those killed since early 1995 in what police believe is a vendetta between nationalists.
